summary: Defines a TLS extension to fix a renegotiation attack in which an attacker connects to a server, injects content, and then splices in a new connection from a victim. The extension cryptographically ties a renegotiation to the earlier handshake. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A trickster could cut into a conversation and make the listener think it was one person talking. This fix lets both sides prove a new conversation continues the old one.

questions: what is the tls renegotiation indication extension
how was the tls renegotiation attack fixed
how does tls prevent the renegotiation attack
subtitle: A TLS extension that ties each renegotiation to the handshake before it, closing a splicing attack.

tldr.problem: TLS renegotiation has no cryptographic link to the earlier handshake, so an attacker can open a connection to a server, inject traffic, and then splice in a client's connection that the server treats as a renegotiation.
tldr.mechanism: Each side saves the verify_data from its Finished message and echoes it in a new renegotiation_info extension on the next handshake, so a mismatch exposes any splice.
tldr.outcome: Renegotiation becomes safe between upgraded peers. Servers SHOULD NOT allow renegotiation without the extension, and many can mitigate the attack simply by refusing to renegotiate at all.

today: RFC 5746 is a Proposed Standard on the standards track. It updates RFC 5246, RFC 4366, RFC 4347, RFC 4346 and RFC 2246, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Renegotiation Attack
sections.content:
TLS lets either side start a renegotiation: a new handshake that establishes new cryptographic parameters. The new handshake runs over the parameters of the old one, but nothing cryptographically binds the two together.

So an attacker who can intercept a client's connection can first form his own TLS connection to the server and send traffic of his choice. He then lets the client's handshake proceed over that connection. The attacker cannot read the client's later traffic, but the server believes the early traffic and the later traffic come from the same party.

With HTTPS and HTTP cookies, the attacker may be able to generate a request of his choice that is validated by the client's cookie. In IMAP or SMTP, a command prefixed by the attacker could make the client's password visible to him.

Protocols that require a round trip to the server over TLS before the client sends sensitive information are likely to be less vulnerable.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person talks to a shopkeeper first, then swaps places with you in the line. The shopkeeper thinks it was all one customer, so the sneaky person's order gets your name on it.

sections.title: State and the renegotiation_info Extension
sections.content:
Both sides store three new values per connection: a secure_renegotiation flag, client_verify_data and server_verify_data. The two verify_data values come from the Finished messages of the immediately previous handshake. For currently defined TLS versions this is 12 bytes each; for SSLv3 it is 36 bytes.

The new extension is renegotiation_info, extension type 0xff01. Its data is a RenegotiationInfo structure holding one field, renegotiated_connection, of 0 to 255 bytes.

  • On an initial handshake the field is empty in both hellos, so the whole extension encodes as ff 01 00 01 00.
  • In a renegotiating ClientHello it holds the client_verify_data.
  • In a renegotiating ServerHello it holds client_verify_data followed by server_verify_data: 24 bytes for current TLS, 72 for SSLv3.

The extension also applies to Datagram TLS (DTLS).
sections.plainLanguage: Each side remembers a short secret code from the last handshake. When they renegotiate, they have to say that code back. A stranger who was not in the first handshake does not know it.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
On the initial handshake the client MUST send either an empty renegotiation_info extension or the signaling cipher suite value described below. If the ServerHello lacks the extension, the client sets secure_renegotiation to FALSE. If it is present, the flag becomes TRUE and the client MUST abort unless the field has zero length. The server mirrors this: it sets the flag on seeing the SCSV or the extension, and then MUST include an empty extension in the ServerHello.

On a secure renegotiation, the client MUST send the extension with its saved client_verify_data and MUST NOT include the SCSV. The server MUST check that the value equals its saved client_verify_data and reply with both saved values. The client then checks that the first half of the reply equals its saved client_verify_data and the second half its saved server_verify_data. Any failed check means aborting the handshake, which is shorthand for a fatal handshake_failure alert followed by closing the connection.

After each completed handshake, both sides save the new verify_data values.
sections.plainLanguage: On the first meeting, both sides just say they know the secret-code game. On later meetings, each must say back the code from last time, and if anything is wrong, they hang up.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and the SCSV
sections.content:
Some SSLv3 and TLS 1.0 implementations wrongly fail a handshake that contains extensions. To work with them, the RFC defines a Signaling Cipher Suite Value, TLS_EMPTY_RENEGOTIATION_INFO_SCSV, with code point {0x00, 0xFF}. It is not a real cipher suite and cannot be negotiated; it means the same as an empty extension. A minimal client that never renegotiates can send just the SCSV on every initial handshake.

When the other side does not support the extension, legacy renegotiation is the only path. Clients are RECOMMENDED to refuse such a request with a no_renegotiation alert, and servers are RECOMMENDED not to permit legacy renegotiation. If they allow it, a server MUST reject a ClientHello carrying the SCSV or the extension, and a client MUST abort if the ServerHello contains the extension.

A client that wants to rule out the attack must terminate whenever the server does not echo the extension. The RFC expects many servers that do not renegotiate (and so are not vulnerable) will not support the extension either, so this choice costs interoperability. Even servers that never renegotiate MUST implement the minimal extension for initial handshakes so clients can probe them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old machines get confused by new words, so there is a quiet way to say the same thing that old machines ignore. Careful people can refuse to talk to anyone who does not answer the secret-code game.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension prevents the splicing attack. Without it, the injected conversation is invisible to the client and looks like an ordinary renegotiation to the server. Servers SHOULD NOT allow clients to renegotiate without using this extension, and TLS implementations SHOULD provide a way to disable and enable renegotiation.

The extension does not solve every problem. During renegotiation either side can present a different certificate than before, which an application might not expect and might handle insecurely. Implementations are encouraged to document how renegotiation affects their APIs and may offer an option to abort if the peer authenticates with a different certificate or server name. Turning such options on by default could break applications that use renegotiation to switch certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret-code trick stops the stranger from cutting in. But if the other person quietly changes their ID card halfway through, a careless program might not notice.
